Expectation1: Officiate at life cycle events such as weddings, bar/bat mitzvahs, and funerals.
Situation1: A congregant has just passed away and the family needs him to officiate the funeral service very soon.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They confront a systemic issue that immediately affects the rights or safety of vulnerable groups and requires urgent institutional response.
Story: I sat in my study, the phone still warm in my hand after speaking with Miriam, whose father had just passed away. Her voice trembled as she asked if I could lead the funeral service tomorrow. As their rabbi, I knew how much it would mean for me to be there, to guide them through their grief, to honor the memory of a beloved member of our community. Yet, even as I tried to comfort her, my inbox pinged with an urgent message from the advocacy group I work with. A new policy was being rushed through the city council—one that would strip protections from the very people I’ve spent years defending. The meeting to challenge it was scheduled for the same time as the funeral. My heart pounded as I weighed the expectations: to be a source of comfort and tradition for a grieving family, or to stand up and fight for justice for those whose voices are so often ignored. Both roles called to the deepest parts of who I am, but in this moment, I could not be in two places at once. I closed my eyes, feeling the weight of both worlds pressing in, unsure which path I would choose.
